a: Arrays give O(1) index access; linked lists give O(1) insert/delete at known nodes but O(n) access.
Each node has next and prev pointers, enabling bidirectional traversal.
A ring buffer reuses a fixed array with head/tail indices for queues.
A collision is when two keys hash to the same bucket; resolved by chaining or open addressing.
A Bloom filter is a probabilistic set: may false-positive, never false-negative (for membership).
A trie (prefix tree) stores strings by shared prefixes for fast prefix search.
Adjacency lists store neighbors per vertex — efficient for sparse graphs.
Adjacency matrices use a V×V matrix — efficient for dense graphs and O(1) edge checks.
A priority queue serves the highest (or lowest) priority element first, often via a heap.
AVL is a self-balancing BST keeping height difference at most 1.
Red-black trees are self-balancing BSTs used in many language standard libraries.
B-trees are multi-way balanced trees optimized for disk/database indexes.
A skip list uses layered linked lists for probabilistic logarithmic search.
Union-Find (DSU) tracks disjoint sets with near-O(1) union and find.
A segment tree answers range queries and updates efficiently (e.g. range sum).
